title: Establishing Battery Supply Chain Resilience for Drones
gist: The authors argue drone batteries are becoming part fuel, part munition and part industrial vulnerability, and propose a three-part resilience approach: a strategic battery reserve, domestic and allied cell supply chains, and advanced chemistry R&D, noting defense is a small price-taker in the battery market.

insights.claim: Benchmark Mineral Intelligence estimates defense batteries consumed 4.3 GWh in 2025 against roughly 1.6 TWh across all uses, with drones making up 39 percent of defense battery demand.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: Defense is a negligible fraction of lithium-ion demand, so it cannot move the market.

insights.claim: The Drone Dominance Program is moving from tens of thousands of low-cost one-way attack drones in 2026 toward more than 200,000 by 2027, prioritizing non-Chinese supply.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: A fivefold ramp in drone volume drives domestic and allied cell demand.
insights.locator: The Department of Defense's Drone Dominance Program

insights.claim: The commercial battery market is two to three orders of magnitude larger than military demand, so defense cannot solve the problem just by buying more and must ride commercial scale where interruption is tolerable.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: Commercial EV and storage dynamics, not defense budgets, set cell availability and price.
insights.locator: Consequently, defense is a price taker

insights.claim: A drone battery is simultaneously like fuel for reusable drones, an expended part of one-way attack drones, and a shelf-life-limited component of loitering munitions, making batteries part of a formation's combat consumption rate.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: Batteries should be planned like fuel and munitions in logistics.
insights.locator: A drone battery can occupy three logistical categories

insights.claim: The authors propose a rotating strategic battery reserve, with standardized form factors and continuous replenishment, to cover the interval between supply interruption and restored qualified production.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: A reserve would create steady defense-specific demand for qualified cells.

insights.claim: Recharging in combat is difficult: generators create signatures, charging times and spare-pack ratios cap sortie rates, and a fixed charging node can be as vulnerable as a fuel point; Ukraine exposed this burden.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: Charging and power-management systems are a logistics bottleneck for drone-heavy forces.
insights.locator: Refueling, even in an electrical sense

insights.claim: FY2024 NDAA Section 154 bars the Defense Department from Oct. 1, 2027 from procuring batteries from CATL, BYD, Envision Energy, EVE Energy, Gotion High-Tech, Hithium or their successors.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: Oct. 1, 2027 is a hard date for Chinese cell exclusion in defense; non-Chinese cell makers gain.

insights.claim: A battery assembled by a US or allied firm can still rely on Chinese cells, anode or cathode materials, electrolyte, processed lithium or graphite, or equipment; domestic assembly is not supply chain independence.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: Look through to upstream materials when evaluating 'domestic' battery claims.

insights.claim: A 2025 GAO report found Pentagon mapping gave better insight into primes and upper-tier suppliers than raw materials and deeper tiers; the MQ-9's visible suppliers appeared US and European while a separate analysis found Chinese integration at sub-tiers.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: Hidden sub-tier Chinese content is a systemic risk in defense hardware.
insights.locator: The Government Accountability Office reported in 2025

insights.claim: The authors recommend a tiered approach: low-consequence, quick-recovery dependencies ride commercial scale; concentrated high-consequence ones need multiple pre-qualified US or allied sources; long-recovery, defense-specific ones need protected capacity via long-term contracts, capacity reservations or sovereign production.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: Capacity reservations and offtake contracts are likely tools; beneficiaries are qualified US/allied cell makers.

insights.claim: Lithium-sulfur, silicon-rich anodes, lithium metal, semi-solid, solid-state and metal-air chemistries may reduce reliance on materials concentrated in today's lithium-ion chain, but only if the industrial base is designed for them.
insights.speaker: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
insights.so_what: Emerging chemistries are a defense-funded R&D angle, not near-term supply.

source_meta.author: Morgan Bazilian, Alex Gilbert, and Aashutosh Mistry
